This interactive map renders fully when deployed to GitHub Pages or opened locally. All crash data, markers, corridors, and tools are loaded — they just need a basemap.

Not on the map: 17,851 of 273,484 crashes (6.5%) have no usable coordinates in the NYC Open Data records. They are counted in every total and chart on this page.

About this map and your privacy

Not shown as hotspots: crashes that the source logged to a road or a default address, with no specific location (Verrazano Bridge: 231, Triborough Bridge: 217, Verrazano Bridge Upper: 100, Brooklyn Bridge: 54, Laurelton Parkway: 36, Verrazano Bridge Lower: 32, Martin Luther King Jr: 15, Bronx Whitestone Bridge: 15, and 1 other roads: 15). They are counted in every total and chart on this page.

Privacy: This page has no backend, no analytics, and no cookies, and nothing you type is stored by crashmaps. Loading it fetches fonts from Google Fonts, scripts from cdnjs (Cloudflare) and map tiles from CARTO, and each of those services sees your IP address. An address you search is sent to OpenStreetMap Nominatim, and commute start and end points are sent to the public OSRM routing server. Those requests are subject to each service’s privacy policy.

13 — Sources

Where This Data Comes From

NYC Open Data
Motor Vehicle Collisions dataset from NYPD, updated daily. 85,559 citywide crash records for 2025.

NYC Open Data →
NYC Vision Zero
New York City adopted Vision Zero in 2014 — the first major US city to do so.

Vision Zero →
NYPD Traffic Data
Crash reports filed via NYPD form MV-104AN for collisions involving injury, death, or property damage exceeding $1,000.

NYPD Traffic →
14 — Methodology

How I Built This

Data pipeline: Crash records queried from NYC Open Data Socrata API (dataset h9gi-nx95), paginated at 50,000 records per call. 85,559 citywide records for 2025. Coordinates are native WGS84 — no reprojection needed.
Borough assignment: Borough comes from the NYC borough field. When that field is blank, the borough is assigned from the crash coordinates using NYC’s official borough boundaries (water areas included). Crashes with neither a borough nor coordinates are counted under “Borough not recorded”: they stay in every citywide total and are left off the map.
Data note: Earlier versions of this dashboard dropped every record with a blank borough field, which undercounted 2022–2024 crashes by about 30% (and fatal crashes by about 40%). Since November 2026 those records are placed by their coordinates, so every year is counted the same way.
Behavioral flags: Impairment and speed derived from contributing factor fields (5 per crash). "Alcohol Involvement" and "Drugs (illegal)" map to impairment; "Unsafe Speed" maps to speed-related. Hit-and-run data is not available in this dataset.
Why this count differs from NYC DOT’s: The 229 deaths shown for 2025 are the sum of “persons killed” across every police-reported collision in the NYC Open Data table, which NYPD describes as preliminary and subject to change. NYC DOT counted 205 traffic deaths for 2025 in its year-end release (January 2026). DOT’s figure comes from a separate fatality database that DOT maintains and reconciles with NYPD records; later DOT publications put 2025 at 209 (April 2026) and 210 (Vision Zero View, November 2026). Neither agency publishes which cases are in one count and missing from the other, so the two totals cannot be matched record by record. For the city’s official count, use Vision Zero View (vzv.nyc).
Hotspots: A hotspot is every crash within roughly a 200-metre area. 31 of the 65 hotspots on this page come from records that give a street with no cross street. Those are grouped by 200-metre square and labelled “[street] near [nearest cross street]”, with the cross street taken from OpenStreetMap. The count covers every crash in the square, including crashes on the other streets inside it. Squares next to each other are listed separately.
Records with no street text: 75,248 crashes have coordinates and no street or intersection text in the source records. They are counted in the hotspot at their coordinates. A hotspot’s name comes from the records in it that do carry text, or from OpenStreetMap when none does.
Hotspot review: 715 crashes are recorded at 19 coordinates where the source logged crashes to a whole road or a default address, so the coordinate does not show where each crash happened. A coordinate is left out automatically when every address on it is a road name alone, with no block number or cross street, on 15 or more crashes, and that road’s crashes sit on a few points (fewer than 20 coordinates for the whole road, or one coordinate holding a fifth of them); I reviewed the others by hand. A road whose crashes are spread over many coordinates along its length stays in. They are left out of the Top 10 and the map hotspots and are counted in every total; “About this map and your privacy” under the map lists them.
